# Finding and Fixing an Error

:::{.callout-note title="Draft"}
First draft, 2026-10-22, from the outline of the same day. Every number in the text is computed when the book builds. Needs dev dplR 1.8.1 for the ring-edit methods and `xdate.report`. Open questions are in the backlog.
:::

## Big Idea

[Crossdating a Collection](05Crossdating.qmd) ended with two flagged series in Mesa Verde, each error placed within a 50-year segment. This chapter takes an error from a segment to a year, puts the ring back, and checks the result. The order of work doesn't change from one collection to the next. Narrow the window with the statistics, look at the core, make the edit, run the report again. The statistics never make the edit on their own. Pilcher put it plainly in the methods book most of us call the Cook Book: a computer makes crossdating faster and easier, and it doesn't make it any better [@Pilcher1990].

A word about expectations first. Mesa Verde is about as good as correlations get in dendrochronology. Everything in the last chapter worked cleanly because those trees agree so well, and if that's all you see you'll expect too much of your own collection. So Mesa Verde gets one short section here. Most of the chapter is about Hurricane Ridge, an ordinary collection that as far as anyone knows is dated correctly, and about the simulated stand, where we know the answer. The second half is about flags nobody planted, because in most collections most flags are not dating errors, and telling which ones are is the skill.

## Packages


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplR)
source("R/plant-dating-errors.R")
source("R/sim-collection.R")
co021 <- read.rwl("data/co021.rwl", format = "tucson")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
wa082 <- read.rwl("data/wa082.rwl", format = "tucson")
```

`co021Bad` is Mesa Verde with the two errors from the last chapter. `wa082Bad` is Hurricane Ridge with one: series 712031 has lost its 1850 ring.

## The Clean Case, Briefly

`corr.series.seg` takes one series and correlates its segments with a master built from the others, and adds a running correlation underneath.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
css645 <- corr.series.seg(co021Bad, series = "645221", seg.length = 50)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Series 645221 in Mesa Verde, with its 1797 ring deleted. Horizontal bars are 50-year segments, the curve is a running correlation, and the dashed line is the critical value.](06FixingErrors_files/figure-html/fix-css-645221-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


That's the report's row for 645221 drawn at a finer grain. The correlation sits near zero until the late 1700s and then climbs to where the rest of the collection lives. Somewhere in the climb is the missing ring.

`ccf.series.rwl` goes the rest of the way. It cuts the series into short segments, here 20 years overlapping by 10, and correlates each with the master at a range of lags. Cut the collection down to the years around the problem with `window` first. What comes back is a table of correlations, one column for each 20-year segment and one row for each lag, here 11 rows by 14 columns. Rather than read all of them, a three-line helper, `bestLag`, picks out the lag with the highest correlation in each column. The rest of the chapter uses it too.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ccf645 <- ccf.series.rwl(window(co021Bad, 1700, 1850), series = "645221",
                         seg.length = 20, bin.floor = 0, make.plot = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Negative lags suggest a missing ring in the series 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# ccf645$ccf is a table with one column per 20-year bin and one row per lag,
# named "lag.-5" to "lag.5". For each column, find the row with the highest
# correlation and turn its name into a number.
bestLag <- function(ccfResult) {
  lags <- as.numeric(sub("lag.", "", rownames(ccfResult$ccf)))
  apply(ccfResult$ccf, 2, function(column) lags[which.max(column)])
}
bestLag(ccf645)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
1700.1719 1710.1729 1720.1739 1730.1749 1740.1759 1750.1769 1760.1779 1770.1789 
       -1        -1        -1        -1        -1        -1        -1        -1 
1780.1799 1790.1809 1800.1819 1810.1829 1820.1839 1830.1849 
       -1         0         0         0         0         0 
```


:::
:::




Every bin through 1780 to 1799 lines up best at lag -1, with correlations around 0.87, and every bin from 1790 to 1809 onward lines up at lag 0, around 0.93. The years those two bins share, the 1790s, are where the ring went missing, and the ring I deleted was 1797. The same treatment of 643143, the false ring, has its last bin at lag +1 in 1412 to 1431 and its first at lag 0 in 1422 to 1441, which puts the error in the 1420s. The planted year is 1425. A negative lag is a missing ring and a positive one is a false ring, as in the last chapter.

Correlations near 0.9 in 20-year bins are what Mesa Verde gives you. Now look at an ordinary collection.

## An Ordinary Collection


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
wa082Report <- xdate.report(wa082Bad)
wa082Flags <- wa082Report$flagged
wa082Flags[, c("series", "from", "to", "flag", "r.dated", "best.lag", "r.lag", "weak")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  series from   to flag     r.dated best.lag     r.lag  weak
1 712022 1850 1899    B  0.15104137       -9 0.3097862  TRUE
2 712022 1875 1924    B  0.10646808       -9 0.3033917  TRUE
3 712031 1775 1824    B  0.12038963       -1 0.5281842 FALSE
4 712031 1800 1849    B -0.13893577       -1 0.6175002 FALSE
5 712031 1825 1874    A  0.30463169        0        NA FALSE
6 712041 1725 1774    B  0.09380315       -8 0.2397792  TRUE
7 712061 1800 1849    A  0.30329539        0        NA FALSE
8 712071 1900 1949    A  0.30460879        0        NA FALSE
9 712122 1925 1974    B  0.24358211        8 0.3150181  TRUE
```


:::
:::




The planted error is there: 712031 is flagged B at lag -1 in two segments, with correlations of 0.53 and 0.62 at the lag, and then A in 1825 to 1874. That A is the segment that straddles the error, half misdated and half not, so it fits badly where it is and no better anywhere else. It's the commonest way a real error shows up at the end of its run of B flags. And it isn't alone. Six other segments are flagged in series that nobody touched, which is how a real error usually looks: one problem among several things that look like problems.

Here is `ccf.series.rwl` on 712031, drawn this time.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ccf031 <- ccf.series.rwl(window(wa082Bad, 1790, 1910), series = "712031",
                         seg.length = 20, bin.floor = 0)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Negative lags suggest a missing ring in the series 
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Cross-correlations of 712031 with the master in 20-year bins overlapping by 10, from 1790 to 1910. Read the panels from the bottom left, along each row and then up. Dashed lines are the critical value.](06FixingErrors_files/figure-html/fix-ccf-712031-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::




It works, but look at the difference from Mesa Verde. At lag -1 the early bins correlate between 0.42 and 0.75. One bin, 1842 to 1861, points nowhere useful: its best lag is -2, at only 0.34, which is no dating error anyone planted. It's what a bin straddling an error looks like when the signal is ordinary. From the 1852 to 1871 bin on, lag 0 wins at 0.51 to 0.82. The last bin at lag -1 is 1832 to 1851 and the first at lag 0 is 1852 to 1871, with the muddled bin between them, so the error is somewhere from the 1840s to the early 1850s. The planted year is 1850. Short segments trade reliability for resolution, and at Hurricane Ridge 20 years is near the edge. With 30-year bins the last bin at lag -1 is 1822 to 1851 and the first at lag 0 is 1837 to 1866. No bin points anywhere else, and the years the two share hold the error.

The last statistical step is the one Douglass would recognize. `xskel.ccf.plot` draws a skeleton plot of the series above one of the master for a window of years, with the cross-correlations for each half underneath.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
xskel.ccf.plot(wa082Bad, series = "712031", win.start = 1830, win.width = 40)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Skeleton plots of 712031 (top) and the master (bottom) for 1830 to 1870, with cross-correlations for each 20-year half. Long bars are narrow rings.](06FixingErrors_files/figure-html/fix-xskel-712031-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Look at the marker years, the narrow rings that get long bars. Before 1850 the series' markers fall one year after the master's: 1836 against 1835, 1841 against 1840. After it, 1852, 1864 and 1866 line up in both. Something happened in 712031 around 1850, and the master has a narrow ring in 1850, which is exactly the kind of year a ring goes missing in.

That is as far as the statistics go. The next step is the core. On a mounted, sanded core you'd look at the rings around 1850 under the microscope for a ring that pinches out or a micro ring squeezed against its neighbor. The other core from the same tree is the first thing to check against, since it should share the tree's missing rings and its own dating stands or falls separately. For a false ring you'd look for a density change inside a ring that doesn't end in a sharp boundary. Pilcher's account of crossdating is good on all of this, and on the error that has nothing to do with the tree: a decade miscounted when the measurements were written down, which is what the dots every ten years on a mounted core are for [@Pilcher1990, p. 45].

## Putting the Rings Back

`insert.ring` and `delete.ring` take the collection, the series and the year.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
co021Fixed <- insert.ring(co021Bad, series = "645221", year = 1797, ring.value = 0)
co021Fixed <- delete.ring(co021Fixed, series = "643143", year = 1425)
wa082Fixed <- insert.ring(wa082Bad, series = "712031", year = 1850, ring.value = 0)
```
:::




Inserting a ring of zero width says the ring is locally absent on this radius, which is what a missing ring found on the core usually is. The dates come back exactly: 645221 and 712031 run over the same years they did before I broke them. The width doesn't. The ring I deleted from 645221 was 0.25 mm wide, and nothing in the statistics could have told you that. They find where a ring is missing and say nothing about how wide it was. Only the sample, or another radius from the same tree, can say.

Deleting the 1425 ring puts 643143 back exactly. So would deleting 1424, because the false ring I planted is a copy of its neighbor. Which of two rings is the false one is a question for the core under a microscope.

Both functions hold the outer year fixed and move the rings inside it, which is what you want for a core from a living tree, where the outer ring is the year you cored it. A floating series has no year to hold, and [Dating a Floater](07Floaters.qmd) deals with that.

Now check the work.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nrow(xdate.report(co021Fixed)$flagged)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
wa082FixedFlags <- xdate.report(wa082Fixed)$flagged
unique(wa082FixedFlags$series)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "712022" "712041" "712061" "712071" "712122"
```


:::
:::


Mesa Verde has no flags. Hurricane Ridge is back to its own six, none of them in 712031. And keep the script. Those three lines are the record of what you changed and why, attached to the original file. xDateR writes the same kind of record for you when you edit there.

## Flags Nobody Planted

So what about Hurricane Ridge's other flags? Before deciding, practice on a collection where the answer is known. The simulated stand from [Chapter 2](02CoresToRecord.qmd) has one dating error, a missing ring in SIM03A at 1800, and nothing else.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sim <- sim.collection(seed = 1)
simFlags <- xdate.report(sim$rwl)$flagged
simFlags[, c("series", "from", "to", "flag", "r.dated", "best.lag", "r.lag", "gain", "weak")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  series from   to flag    r.dated best.lag     r.lag       gain  weak
1 SIM03A 1725 1774    B -0.2119268       -1 0.6309792 0.84290597 FALSE
2 SIM03A 1750 1799    B -0.2544623       -1 0.5605399 0.81500220 FALSE
3 SIM03A 1775 1824    B  0.2266457        1 0.2910696 0.06442389  TRUE
4 SIM10A 1900 1949    B  0.2934495       -9 0.3281379 0.03468835 FALSE
```


:::
:::




SIM03A looks like 712031: B flags at lag -1 with gains of 0.84 and 0.82 in the segments before the error. The segment that straddles it, 1775-1824, is flagged too, at lag +1 with a gain of only 0.06, and it is marked weak. In 712031 the same segment got an A. Either way the report is saying the same thing: half of the segment is dated right and half is a year off, so no single shift fits it.

SIM10A is the one that is dated correctly, and I know because I built it. Its segment from 1900 to 1949 correlates with the master at 0.293 where it is dated, a little under the critical value of 0.328, and shifted 9 years it correlates at 0.328, right at it. The gain is 0.035. For that shift to be real, the core would need nine rings missing inside one 50-year segment and none anywhere else. A segment that fits poorly where it is, and only slightly better at a shift no core could plausibly need, is noise.

Now Hurricane Ridge as it comes.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
wa082Flags0 <- xdate.report(wa082)$flagged
wa082Flags0[, c("series", "from", "to", "flag", "r.dated", "best.lag", "r.lag", "weak")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  series from   to flag   r.dated best.lag     r.lag  weak
1 712022 1850 1899    B 0.1507769       -9 0.3102281  TRUE
2 712022 1875 1924    B 0.1063661       -9 0.3033725  TRUE
3 712041 1725 1774    B 0.1089703       -8 0.2386636  TRUE
4 712061 1800 1849    A 0.3060106        0        NA FALSE
5 712071 1900 1949    A 0.3047195        0        NA FALSE
6 712122 1925 1974    B 0.2434454        8 0.3150051  TRUE
```


:::
:::




The four B flags are all marked weak, at lags of -9, -9, -8, +8. A misdated core can be off by more than a ring, but a shift of eight or nine years in a segment that fits no better there than anywhere else looks like SIM10A again: a big shift for a small gain. The two A flags, in 712061 and 712071, correlate at 0.306 and 0.305 against a critical value of 0.328. That is low agreement just under a line, in a collection whose segments are often not far above it, and both are best where they're dated. As far as anyone knows, Hurricane Ridge is dated correctly, and nothing here argues otherwise.

What, then, makes a B flag worth pulling a core out of the drawer for? A gain of a few tenths. A lag of one or two years. A run of segments that agree on the lag, and a clean switch back to lag 0 where the run ends, often with an A flag on the segment in between. 712031's planted ring has all of that. None of the flags nobody planted has any of it. In a collection as strong as Mesa Verde even a lone B flag deserves a look, and in an ordinary one I'd wait for the pattern before pulling anything.

## Wrapping Up

The statistics placed every planted error to within a decade or so, the skeleton plot showed the shift in the marker years, and `insert.ring` and `delete.ring` put the rings back with the outer year held fixed. The statistics couldn't say how wide a missing ring was or which of two rings was the false one, and on Hurricane Ridge they flagged six segments in a collection with no known errors. Those are questions for the sample.

The next chapter, [Dating a Floater](07Floaters.qmd), is about a series with no outer year to hold fixed.

## Exercises

1. Narrow 712031 with 10-year segments. Where does it stop being reliable? Do the same for 645221 at Mesa Verde and compare.
2. Insert the missing ring in 645221 with `ring.value = mean(co021Bad[["645221"]], na.rm = TRUE)` instead of zero, detrend, and compare `rwi.stats` with the zero version. Does the choice of width matter for anything downstream?
3. Look at SIM10A's flagged segment with `ccf.series.rwl` and `xskel.ccf.plot`. Would you have pulled the core?
4. Pick one of Hurricane Ridge's A flags and decide what you'd do about it. Does the other core from the same tree help?
5. Plant a missing ring in a weak simulated stand, `sim.collection(rbar.bt = 0.2, rbar.wt = 0.4, seed = 1)`, and try to find it with this chapter's tools.

## Further Reading

- @Pilcher1990 is the chapter on sample preparation, crossdating and measurement in *Methods of Dendrochronology*. It is short and practical: how to prepare a core, how to crossdate it, the decade error, and why you shouldn't expect to crossdate a sequence much shorter than about 40 years.
- @GrissinoMayer2001 walks through what to do with each part of COFECHA's output, including the flagged segments.
- @Black2016 shows what errors that slip through do to a chronology downstream.
